headline: SpaceX Wins Crane Game, Catches Returning Starship With Giant Robot Claw
subheadline: *After an aborted first attempt, engineers confirm the claw 'performed to specification'; the machine dispensed no tickets.*
author: Marisol Vega, Aerospace & Amusements Desk
seoTitle: SpaceX Catches Starship With Giant Robot Claw
seoDescription: Satire: SpaceX caught its returning Starship in giant robot arms after an aborted attempt, proving the aerospace crane game can, in fact, be won.
sourceEvent: SpaceX's Starship completed a successful return to Earth on Saturday and was caught mid-air by the giant mechanical arms of its launch tower in Texas, after an earlier recovery attempt was aborted. It was the first mid-air catch of a returning vehicle of its kind.

social.x: BREAKING: SpaceX has won the crane game. Starship caught mid-air by giant robot arms after one warm-up attempt. The claw, sources confirm, does work — provided you are the player, the arcade owner, and the claw manufacturer.
social.facebook: SpaceX's Starship returned from orbit on Saturday and was plucked out of the sky by two giant robot arms — the first confirmed instance of anyone, anywhere, actually winning a crane game. The catch followed an earlier aborted attempt, described as the aerospace equivalent of the claw gripping firmly and then releasing at the top of its travel for no reason. The machine dispensed no tickets.
social.linkedin: Saturday's successful mid-air catch of Starship is a milestone in vertical integration: SpaceX now controls the player, the arcade, and the claw. Our full analysis of the emerging prize-recovery sector, and what it means for the billion-quarters capex model, below.
social.instagram: They caught a rocket with a giant arcade claw. After one warm-up grab. Somewhere, a man who has spent $340 trying to win a plush dolphin would like a word. #satire #spacex #starship #cranegame #space
altHeadlines: After One Warm-Up Grab, SpaceX's Billion-Dollar Claw Machine Finally Pays Out
Nation's Arcade Patrons Vindicated as SpaceX Proves Claw 'Does Actually Work'

body:
BOCA CHICA, Texas — SpaceX's Starship returned from orbit on Saturday and was snatched out of mid-air by a pair of giant robot arms, marking the first time in recorded history that a player has actually won a crane game.

The launch tower, nicknamed 'Mechazilla' by engineers in what they insist is a technical designation, closed its two steel arms around the returning vehicle as it descended toward the Texas coast — a manoeuvre industry experts described as 'finally, a successful claw drop'.

The catch came after an earlier recovery attempt was aborted, which mission officials characterised as the aerospace equivalent of the claw descending perfectly, gripping firmly, and then releasing at the top of its travel for reasons no one will ever be able to explain.

'The machine performed exactly to specification,' a SpaceX spokesperson said, while reportedly feeding another four tokens into a slot marked DO NOT SHAKE. 'We budgeted for two plays. One to establish dominance. One to win. That is how the game is played.'

Engineers confirmed the arms operate on the same principle as the seaside arcade claw machine, with three minor differences: the prize weighs several hundred tonnes, it arrives at terminal velocity in a halo of superheated plasma, and the machine costs roughly one billion quarters.

'What SpaceX has essentially done,' said one aerospace analyst, 'is spend a decade and a modest nation's GDP proving that the claw does, in fact, work — provided you are simultaneously the player, the arcade owner, and the manufacturer of the claw.'

The breakthrough has prompted soul-searching among the machine's traditional user base. 'So you're telling me it CAN grab things,' said local man Gary Pruitt, 52, who has spent an estimated $340 and much of his marriage attempting to extract a plush dolphin from the machine at his local pier arcade. 'Interesting.'

Rival operators moved quickly to respond. Blue Origin confirmed its own claw machine remains in 'early-stage testing', and is currently at the developmental phase where the claw does not yet reach the prize area. NASA, meanwhile, announced preliminary plans to install giant arms over the Pacific to catch the International Space Station when it retires — or, failing that, a medium-sized bear, for morale.

Regulators noted the catch marks the first aerospace licence to include the clause 'winner takes all', and confirmed the machine dispensed no tickets.

At press time, the tower had reportedly opened its arms and dropped the vehicle the final two feet, in accordance with tradition.
